source.title: Reading Without a Reader: Large Language Models Collapse Reading and Writing into a Single Entangled Code

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures similarity between a single model’s input embedding and output unembedding, not similarity between representations induced by different models on the same inputs. Its scale and metric results therefore do not test any listed version of the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports internal input/output-code similarity and its scale trajectory. These are related to representational alignment but are not comparisons between models’ representations. Its behavioural read/write tests are explicitly withdrawn; cited findings from other work are not recorded as results. Other experiments in the paper concern different topics.
record.test_reason: The study compares one model's input embedding (WE) with its own output unembedding (WU). It never compares representations of different models, seeds or modalities on shared inputs. It cites Huh et al. (2024) only as the source of the mutual k-NN metric. Its scale trend (n=6 Pythia) concerns within-model WE/WU similarity, not cross-model convergence, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that untied Pythia WE/WU codes are coupled but sub-ceiling, follow a couple-then-differentiate trajectory with asymmetric WU drift (replicating Lopardo et al.), and show a flat, underpowered scale trend. They also say the behavioural comprehension/production dissociation test cannot be validly run at the output. They withdraw the coupling statistic, the geometry→behaviour bridge and the encoder/decoder separation measure. They make no cross-model convergence claim.
record.recipe_differences: Measures input-embedding/output-unembedding similarity within individual models, rather than comparing representations across models on shared inputs; uses CKA, Procrustes/cosine and mutual k-NN with floor, shuffled-token null and tied ceiling.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports several complementary similarity measures but does not report a systematic sweep of metric settings or input datasets for this within-model alignment result.

fits_no_version.finding: In untied Pythia models (14m–1.4b), WE/WU composite E is 0.226–0.349. This is far above an independent-init floor and below the tied ceiling. There is no systematic scale trend (Spearman 0.37, p=0.49, n=6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within a decoder-only LM, untied input and output token codes are partially aligned, and this alignment does not grow systematically with size.

fits_no_version.finding: In pythia-160m, WE/WU CKA goes 0.015 → 0.494 (step 4000) → 0.210 (final step), with WU drifting about 3.2× more than WE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-model input/output-code alignment follows a couple-then-differentiate trajectory during training.

record.problems: The cross-size trend uses only n = 6 and is described as underpowered; model-family and tokenizer differences confound tied-versus-untied comparisons. The tied values are imposed by construction, not learned findings. The paper itself cautions that WE/WU are an analogy to reading/writing systems, not a measurement of separate reading and writing networks.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the frequency-decile drift results and the other experiments because they do not measure representational alignment of the kind relevant to the claim. The paper reports asymmetric WE/WU weight drift in Section 4.7 and Table B11, but drift is not a similarity/alignment result between models. The encoder/decoder representational-separation analysis is explicitly withdrawn in Section 4.8.

untested.parts: No comparison of independently trained models' representations, and no cross-model alignment trend with scale.
No vision-language or paired image-caption comparison.
No comparison of networks trained from different seeds.
No cross-model mapping or stitching. The Procrustes map is fitted between WE and WU within a single model.
No analysis of features or circuits recurring across models.
No test of whether cross-model convergence depends on the metric or the inputs.
No test of incompleteness or causes of cross-model alignment.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': the Platonic Representation Hypothesis paper is cited only as the source of the mutual k-NN metric, and convergence is not discussed as a claim. The Exp. 9 encoder/decoder 1−CKA separation compares two stacks within one model and is withdrawn, so it is not relevant. The Exp. 6 comparison of hidden-state geometry with perceptual norms is also not cross-model.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare representations across independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, data, or modalities.
No paired image-caption or other vision-language comparison.
No comparison across training seeds or analysis of shared features/subspaces across independently initialized networks.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test between models.
No cross-model recurrence analysis of interpretable features or circuits.

Uses several similarity measures for within-model input/output codes, but does not test whether convergence between models varies with metric settings or input data, or disappears out of distribution.
Does not test whether cross-model alignment is incomplete or explained by shared training data/objectives rather than a common model of reality.

relation.reason: Huh et al. (2024) is cited for mutual k-NN overlap; the study does not test or substantively discuss the catalog's cross-model convergence claims.

tranche.reason: The study measures input/output-code alignment within individual models. It neither tests cross-model representation convergence nor uses that finding as a tool.

source_check.notes: All listed numerical values match the text. Observed coupling and the scale null concern within-model WE/WU alignment only; none bears on V1–V7, and the underpowered scale null does not establish scale invariance.
